fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: a condition of _strain_, the result of a _stress_, is a direct stimulus to growth itself. This indeed is no less than one of the cardinal facts of theoretical biology.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Strain as a stimulus to growth”. Scope: living tissues of animals and plants, especially bone, skin and supporting plant tissues

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mechanobiological response is measurable, but “direct stimulus” requires causal data and a modern interpretation. Existing experimental datasets test subsets such as bone, while the universal tissue claim remains inadequately covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate experimentally or naturally increased mechanical strain to subsequent tissue growth or thickening using longitudinal controls and dose-response models. Growth without increased strain, or strain without subsequent growth under viable conditions, would challenge the direct mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Hormonal and injury responses confound direct causation.

Load, strain and growth are rarely all measured.

The scope spans very different tissues and kingdoms.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Strain versus later growth is measurable, and a large experimental literature already reports both. Calling the stimulus direct requires controls that most deposited tables do not include, and the public record is a compilation job rather than a single dataset. Existing studies can test the load-growth association in bone for a few species and leave skin, plants and the directness claim only partly constrained.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate a measured increase in mechanical strain to a subsequent increase in tissue growth or thickness, with controls that hold hormones, perfusion and inflammation fixed. Support would be thicker bone, skin or supporting tissue under higher strain in those controls; growth that tracks systemic factors once strain is matched would fail the claim that strain itself is the direct stimulus.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Loading experiments are numerous and scattered across papers, supplements and animal protocols rather than one open archive.

Surgical models such as tibial excision change blood flow and muscle use together with strain.
